newsitem.title: USA: ISSUER FOCUS - Omaha, Neb., eyes economic boom.
newsitem.headline: ISSUER FOCUS - Omaha, Neb., eyes economic boom.

text.p: The good economic news was pouring out of Omaha, Neb., last week.
First, Union Pacific Railroad announced it will add about 1,000 jobs in Nebraska, with an estimated 800 of those jobs slated for Omaha.

"Omaha is our hometown," railroad president Ron Burns said in the announcement. "This decision reinforces our commitment to the community and underscores our intention to keep the railroad headquarters right where it's been for 131 years."

A day later, executives at First National Bank of Omaha and the Omaha World-Herald said they intended to participate in the city's new downtown northeast redevelopment plan, by building new facilities within the plan area. The investment by the two companies reportedly totals about $160 million.

"We chose to stay downtown," said John Gottschalk, president and chief executive officer of the World-Herald, adding that the newly announced developments "will encourage other companies and businesses to consider downtown locations and expansions."
In fact, Brinker Harding, assistant to Mayor Hal Daub for community growth, said more downtown development announcements are expected.
"Things are really just booming," said Jay Noddle, president of Pacific Realty Group Inc, coordinator for the First National Bank of Omaha project.

To spur that boom, Omaha has offered incentives such as $18 million to $20 million in infrastructure work, according to Lou D'Ercole, the city's finance director. He said the city has various options for financing street and sewer work, as well as parking garages within the redevelopment plan.

Those include lease revenue bonds for the parking garages. Omaha also has $50 million to $60 million of unused, voter-approved GO bond authorization that can be tapped for infrastructure improvements, D'Ercole said.
In addition, tax increment financing could be used for infrastructure or to aid in land acquisition or clearing, he added.
In return, Omaha, which already enjoys a low unemployment rate, gets more jobs and a revitalized downtown, D'Ercole said.
The problem is Omaha has no upward mobility when it comes to to debt ratings.

The city's $153 million of outstanding general obligation debt is rated triple-A by both Moody's Investors Service and Standard & Poor's Corp. The city is one of only a handful of city credits with triple-A ratings from both agencies.
"(Omaha) is a very strong credit, in large part due to good management and the health of the local economy," said Mitchell Savader, a rating analyst at Moody's.
But there is a downside to the city's robust economic health, Savader said, and that is a growing scarcity of labor to fill the new jobs.
"Companies have sometimes aggressively recruited from out of state," he said.

Omaha has had some financial challenges as well, according to Robert Durante, a director at Standard & Poor's. The city's budget balance over the last couple of years slipped below 10 percent of expenditures and city officials are working to bring the balance back up.
As for last week's economic news, Durante said that "on one hand it's the type of announcement you'd expect from a triple-A credit."
"It's obviously good news for the city," he added.
